newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Havel to announce decision on new term on Saturday.
newsitem.headline: Havel to announce decision on new term on Saturday.

text.p: Czech President Vaclav Havel, a fixture in Prague Castle since helping lead 1989's peaceful overthrow of the Communist government, is expected to say on Saturday whether he will seek another five-year term in office.
Havel has called a garden news conference for noon on Saturday to announce his decision on whether to stand for the post, elected by parliament, when his term ends in February.
No other candidates have yet to emerge to challenge the former playwright for the job and many Czechs have difficulty even imagining somebody taking the popular Havel's place.

But his battle with lung cancer late last year, a difficult recovery, and his unexpected marriage soon after leaving hospital to a Czech actress, all have people questioning how Havel, 60, wants to spend the rest of his life.

Frantisek Kostlan, a commentator for the daily Lidove Noviny, pleaded with Havel in a column on Thursday headlined "The Necessary Protection of Continuity" to say "yes" to a new five years in office, arguing it would be "therapeutic" for the country.
In an interview with Reuters last week, Havel was asked if expected to fulfil his top foreign policy priority and be the one who signs the NATO accession treaty in 1999:
"It would be nice if I, as the one who announced in Prague the official dissolution of the Warsaw Pact... signed the accession to NATO," he said.
"This is a subject to which I shall have to give careful thought but I also know I shall quite soon have to announce the outcome of this thinking."

Once one of the world's best known chain-smokers, Havel's life changed dramatically during his recovery from the horrific events after his surgery last December, when complications led to a serious case of pneumonia and dangerous fevers.

In a reflective New Year's address even more profound than usual for the humanist philosopher, Havel spoke of his own near-death experience, and the loss of his first wife Olga to cancer less than a year before.
"Both of these experiences, to my own surprise, I have perceived as great challenges for a new and far deeper consideration of the world in which we live."

Havel said that he pondered "about myself, about the mysterious order of human existence, and about the volume of signs or hidden messages which are speaking to us from within this order, which we are mostly ignoring".

Separate camps of doctors feuded over the care he received in a decrepit central Prague surgery clinic -- where Havel insisted on being treated instead of the more luxurious settings of a hospital once reserved for Communist leaders.
Doctors now say that his recovery has gone well, and there have been no hints of the cancer recurring.

He admits to craving cigarettes still, and rails against anyone who suggests he should become an anti-smoking advocate: "Let everyone destroy his or her own health according to his or her own decision," he said in the interview.

Days after he was released from hospital in January, he shocked the country by marrying a well-known stage and screen actress, Dagmar Veskrnova, now 44, who then took the Czech feminine name of Havlova.
Havel was elected to his current term after the split of Czechoslovakia at the beginning of 1993.

Opinion polls show the president, who acts more as a philosophical balancing wheel for the country than a political animal, has maintained the broad popularity which brought him to power after the revolution.
There was however some negative reaction in the local press to his unexpected marriage. Havel bristles at these reports: "It is me, not other people, who will live with my wife."

He frequently battles for the soul of Czech reforms with his long-time right-wing economist prime minister, Vaclav Klaus -- Havel preaching his gospel of the civic society, while Klaus espouses individualism.

Asked if he still felt like a dissident at times alongside a government which carries most of the country's political power, Havel told Reuters: "A careful observer might discern certain dissident features in my behaviour as president."
